Females of Ring-necked duck ultimately attain an adult body mass of 680 grams [Wwi = 680 grams], whereas conspecific males are substantially heavier, reaching an ultimate wet weight of 730 grams [Wwi = 730 grams]. The heavier body mass of males also likely provides a greater buffer against energetic deficits during the wing molt period, when flight is temporarily suspended. Young birds require abundant aquatic invertebrates and plant material to fuel this rapid mass gain, and the productivity of the breeding marsh is a key determinant of whether individuals can reach the adult size range before the autumn migration. This moderately high metabolic rate reflects the species' active foraging lifestyle and its northern breeding distribution, which demands considerable thermoregulatory capacity even during the summer months. The metabolic rate measurement provides a valuable baseline for estimating the daily energy expenditure of free-living birds, particularly during energetically demanding periods such as egg formation and brood rearing.
